title: How To Handle Students Who Push Your Buttons https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/05/23/how-to-handle-students-who-push-your-buttons/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin addresses the common experience of a particular student who reliably irritates a teacher, prompting lectures, arguments, and emotional reactions that only reinforce the unwanted behavior. His central recommendation is disengagement: rather than focusing extra attention, discussion, or negativity on the button-pushing student, the teacher should let the classroom management plan's rules and consequences do the work impartially, treating that student exactly like any other. Linsin predicts that within days of adopting this approach, the student will lose their power to provoke, the teacher will find themselves genuinely warming to the student, and the relationship will transform into one of mutual respect and even affection. He frames this as a reliable, repeatable strategy rather than a one-off trick.
points: Certain students develop an outsized ability to provoke frustration in a teacher, leading to lectures, arguments, and visible irritation that only reinforces the behavior.
The recommended fix is deliberate disengagement: stop fixating on, discussing, or reacting to the student and let established rules and consequences handle accountability impartially.
This shift requires treating the button-pushing student exactly the same as every other student, with no extra attention devoted to their behavior.
Linsin predicts the change happens quickly—within days—and that the teacher's irritation is often replaced by genuine warmth and appreciation for the student.
The strategy is presented as reliably effective 'every time, with every student,' regardless of how annoying the behavior initially seems.
quotes: If you’re like most teachers, you tend to focus on these students, on the one or two with an uncanny ability to push your buttons.
But here’s the thing: These normal reactions are only making things worse. They’re only encouraging more of the same behavior you’d love to avoid.

You need a wide open perspective that includes all students equally. You need to take a step back and allow your rules and consequences to step in and replace in total all your efforts to try and change them.
When you stop focusing on individual students, and instead allow your classroom management plan to do its job, you’ll discover that they no longer have the power to get under your skin.
One day out of the clear blue sky you’ll find yourself smiling at them. Warm and genuine.
This is no pie-in-the-sky scenario. It’s true and it’s real. And it works every time.
